div.head: SUBSECT. 7.
Envy, Malice, Hatred, Causes.
div.p: Envy and Malice, are two links of this chain, and both, as Guainerius Tract. 15 cap. 2, proves out of Galen 3 Aphorism. com. 22, cause this malady by themselves, especially if their bodies be otherwise disposed to Melancholy. ’Tis Valescus de Taranta, and Felix Platerus’ observation, Envy so gnaws many men’s hearts, that they become altogether melancholy. And therefore belike Solomon, Prov. 14. 13, calls it, the rotting of the bones, Cyprian, vulnus occultum [the hidden wound];

the Sicilian tyrants never invented the like torment. It crucifies their souls, withers their bodies, makes them hollow-eyed, His vultus minax, torvus aspectus, pallor in facie, in labiis tremor, stridor in dentibus, &c. [A menacing countenance, a grim look, paleness in the face, quivering lips, grinding teeth, etc.]pale, lean, and ghastly to behold, Cyprian ser. 2 de zelo & livore. As a moth gnaws a garment, so, saith Chrysostom, doth envy consume a man: to be a living Anatomy: a Skeleton, to be a lean and Pallor in ore sedet, macies in corpore toto. Nusquam recta acies, livent rubigine dentes [Pallor is settled in the face, leanness in the whole body. The glance is never direct, the teeth are livid with decay].pale carcass, quickened with a Diaboli expressa Imago, toxicum charitatis, venenum amicitiae, abyssus mentis, non est eo monstrosius monstrum, damnosius damnum, urit, torret, discruciat, macie & squalore conficit [The exact likeness of the devil, the poison of charity, the venom of friendship, the abyss of the mind; there is no more monstrous monster than this, no more injurious injury; it burns, it roasts, it torments, it overcomes with dearth and squalor]. Austin Domin. prima. Advent.fiend, Hall in Charact. For so often as an envious wretch sees another man prosper, to be enriched, to thrive, and be fortunate in the world, to get honours, offices, or the like, he repines and grieves.

lg.l: The successes of men … she is her own punishment.]

div.p:
He tortures himself if his equal, friend, neighbour be preferred, commended, do well, if he understand of it, it galls him afresh, and no greater pain can come to him, than to hear of another man’s well-doing, ’tis a dagger at his heart every such object. He looks at him, as they that fell down in Lucian’s rock of honour, with an envious eye, and will damage himself, to do another a mischief: atque cadet subito, dum super hoste cadat. As he did in Aesop, lose one
eye willingly, that his fellow might lose both, or that rich man in Declam. 13.Quintilian that poisoned the flowers in his garden, because his neighbour’s Bees should get no more honey from them. His whole life is sorrow, and every word he speaks a Satire, nothing fats him but other men’s ruins. For to speak in a word, Envy is naught else but tristitia de bonis alienis, sorrow for other men’s good, be it present, past, or to come: & gaudium de adversis, and Statuis cereis Basilius eos comparat, qui liquefiunt ad praesentiam solis, qua alii gaudent & ornantur. Muscis alii quae ulceribus gaudent amoena praetereunt, sistunt in foetidis [St Basil compares them to wax statues, which melt in the presence of the sun, in so far as others are delighted and adorned. Others, to flies which take pleasure in sores, pass by delightful places and settle in fetid ones].joy at their harms, opposite to mercy, Agrip. lib. 1 cap. 63.which grieves at other men’s mischances, and misaffects the body in another kind; so Damascen defines it, lib. 2 de orthod. fid., Thomas 2. 2 quaest. 36 art. 1, Aristotle lib. 2 Rhet. cap. 4 & 10, Plato Philebo, Tully 3 Tusc., Greg. Nic. lib. de virt. animae cap. 12, Basil. de Invidia, Pindarus Od. 1 ser. 5, and we find it true. ’Tis a common disease, and almost natural to us, as Hist. lib. 2, Tacit.Tacitus holds, to envy another man’s prosperity. And ’tis in most men an incurable disease. I have read, saith Marcus Aurelius, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldee Authors, I have consulted with many wise men, for a remedy for envy, I could find none, but to renounce all happiness, and to be a wretch, and miserable forever. ’Tis the beginning of hell in this life, and a passion not to be excused. Every other sin hath some pleasure annexed to it, or will admit of an excuse; envy alone wants both. Other sins last but for a while, the gut may be satisfied, anger remits, hatred hath an end, envy never ceaseth. Cardan lib. 2 de sap. Divine and human examples are very familiar, you may run and read them, as that of Saul and David, Cain and Abel, angebat illum non proprium peccatum [it wasn’t his own sin that tortured him], sed fratris prosperitas, saith Theodoret, it was his brother’s good fortune galled him. Rachel envied her sister, being barren, Gen. 30, Joseph’s brethren him, Gen. 37, David had a touch of this vice, as he confesseth Urebat me, aemulatio propter stultos [It burned me, the envy of the foolish].Psal. 73, Jer. 12. 1.Jeremy and Hab. 1.Habbakuk, they repined at others’ good, but in the end they corrected themselves. Psal. 75, fret not thyself, &c. Domitian spited Agricola for his worth, that a private man should be so much glorified. Tacit. Hist. lib. 2 part. 6.Caecina was envied of his fellow Citizens, because he was more richly adorned. But of all others, Periturae dolore et invidia, si quem viderint ornatiorem: se in publicum prodiisse [Ready to perish from sorrow and envy, if they see any other woman dressed more elegantly than them in public]. Platina dial. amorum.women are most weak, ob pulchritudinem invidae sunt faeminae [women are envious of beauty] (Musaeus) aut amat, aut odit, nihil est tertium (Granatensis). They love, or hate, no medium amongst them. Implacabiles plerumque laesae mulieres [Wronged women are mostly implacable], Agrippina-like, Ant. Guainerius lib. 2 cap. 8. vit. M. Aurelii.A woman if she see her neighbour more
neat or elegant, richer in tires, Jewels, or apparel, is enraged, and like a Lioness sets upon her husband, rails at her, scoffs at her, and cannot abide her; so the Roman Ladies in Tacitus did at Salonina Caecina’s wife, because she had a better horse, and better furniture, as if she had hurt them with it; they were much offended: in like sort our gentlewomen do at their usual meetings, one repines or scoffs at another’s bravery and happiness. Myrsine an Attic wench, was murdered of her fellows, because she did excel the rest in beauty, Constantine Agricult. lib. 11, cap. 7. Every Village will yield such examples.
